P1: In 2005, a few college friends and I visited Oventik, one of the Zapatista caracoles in Chiapas. We nearly died several times getting there. The mountain road wrapped around cliffs, and our rental car was barely running, which is a great combination when you're on your way to visit a revolution.
P2: In San Cristóbal de las Casas, the only white man we met sat us down in a café and asked us questions so directly that he seemed like a CIA agent. Why were we there? Who did we work with? What were our plans? When were we leaving?
P3: It made us feel important for a minute. We were college kids in a dying rental car, but apparently the empire had questions. 😂
P6: What impressed me most was how they handle authority. They call it mandar obedeciendo, leading by obeying. Representatives carry out what the assembly decided, and they stay answerable to the people who gave them the mandate.
P7: The Zapatistas are also the closest thing to a whole example that I found, because for them autonomy is more than a way of voting. They've built their own education and health care. They run their own justice, collective production and political formation, and they've worked out ways of teaching outsiders. And they coordinate beyond a single village.
P9: In 2023, after a long internal review, the Zapatistas announced they were dissolving the Rebel Zapatista Autonomous Municipalities and the Good Government Juntas. Under their new arrangement, authority moved toward Local Autonomous Governments in each community. Those local governments can coordinate through regional collectives, but the coordinating levels are explicitly described as dependent on the communities. They don't sit above them.
P10: Most institutions pile up layers and offices as they get older. The Zapatistas reviewed theirs and pushed authority down. They didn't put out a leadership book and start a certification program. They changed the system they were actually living in.
P11: I need to restrain my enthusiasm here, though. Zapatista autonomy grew out of Indigenous communities with long histories, who share land struggles, language and kinship, and have defended themselves together for decades. A new ecovillage can't copy the visible diagram and get the trust underneath it right away.
P12: The Zapatistas themselves have warned people against importing or exporting Zapatismo as a ready-made model. Their diagram isn't the useful part. The useful part is how they learn: they build, ask, find out where the practice fails, and change the structure.
P13: They also don't prove my whole economic path, from unpriced internal necessities to a common purse to eliminating outside money. Zapatista communities use collective work to support their schools, clinics, autonomous government and resistance. They also sell products, trade, and receive outside support. What they show is that major necessities and public functions can be taken out of ordinary market purchase and governed collectively. Outside help can build capability. But it can also create gatekeepers and uneven dependence, when the specialist, donor or organization stays indispensable.
P14: For the tenth anniversary of their autonomous governments, the Zapatistas opened the Escuelita. Outsiders lived with families and learned autonomy by taking part in their daily life. Around 1,500 students came to the first sessions, and thousands more came to later ones.
P15: An escuelita can fail by turning into a visitor business, where residents spend their lives performing community for paying outsiders, and the number of guests replaces the number of daughter communities as the measure of success. Making people feel transformed for a week isn't the point. The point is to teach enough of the social and material system that some of them can build it somewhere else.
P16: In my research, I also tried to trace what happened after the Escuelita. I found alumni networks, people bringing practices home, and later organizing. But I didn't find a clean line from an Escuelita student to a newly founded communal institution, with evidence of how that institution's members and their children actually did over time. Zapatista influence was already spreading internationally before the Escuelita, so a later resemblance doesn't prove it came from there. What I'm borrowing is a way of teaching and the ambition to replicate. I'm not claiming the Zapatistas already proved my whole model.
P17: Sociocracy arrives at some similar forms from a very different history, with its circles, consent, distributed authority and links between levels. The resemblance doesn't prove there's a universal formula. But it gives builders another serious system to study, so they don't have to invent their governance in the middle of their first dispute.
